care: Molière's comedies include a hypocrite who pursues his host's wife (Tartuffe), a nobleman who breaks his promises to women (Don Juan), and a guardian raising a girl to be his obedient wife (The School for Wives). The lesson summarizes these plots briefly and without detail. The Miser, The Would-Be Gentleman and The Would-Be Invalid are the easiest places for young readers to start.

young.html: Molière was the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, a French actor and playwright who lived about 350 years ago. He ran his own theater company, wrote the plays, and acted the funniest parts himself. King Louis XIV liked his plays and helped protect him.

Most of Molière's comedies have one person with a silly obsession. There is a miser who loves his money-box more than his children, a man who wants so badly to be fancy that he pays teachers to make him a gentleman, and a man so sure he is sick that he wants to marry his daughter to a doctor. Usually a sensible servant or relative sees the truth and helps everyone else.

In The Would-Be Gentleman, Monsieur Jourdain is delighted to learn from his teacher that there are two ways to talk: poetry and prose. He discovers that he has been speaking prose for more than forty years without knowing it!

young.name: gb-moliere
young.cap: Pick a play to meet its foolish hero, the person who sees clearly, and how it ends.

young.html: Act it out. Molière's plays were made to be performed. With your family, act out this short scene from The Miser: Harpagon finds his money-box gone and runs around shouting “Thieves! Thieves!” and asking everyone (even the audience!) if they took it. Make it as funny as you can. Afterward, talk about why it's funny when someone cares too much about one thing.

full.html: Molière (1622–1673), born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, son of an upholsterer to the royal household, gave up a secure future to become an actor. After years touring the provinces, his company won the favor of Louis XIV in 1658 and settled in Paris. Over the next fifteen years he wrote and starred in a stream of comedies, in verse and in prose, that are still the backbone of the French stage.

Molière held that the purpose of comedy is to correct people's faults by making them laugh. His comic heroes are not wicked so much as ruled by one idea, which blinds them to everything else, while those around them suffer or plot to set things right.

items: The School for Wives (1662). Arnolphe, terrified of being deceived by a clever wife, raises his ward Agnès in complete ignorance so she will be an obedient one. Her innocence works against him: she falls in love with a young man and tells Arnolphe all about it. The Critique of the School for Wives (1663) is Molière's playful reply to his critics.

Tartuffe (1664–69). Orgon takes into his house a man who seems to be a saint but is a hypocrite after his money and his family. Orgon's sensible wife Elmire and the outspoken maid Dorine expose him. The play was banned for five years after religious authorities objected; Molière argued that it mocked false piety, not true piety.
Don Juan (1665). A charming nobleman who breaks every promise and mocks heaven, followed by his worried servant Sganarelle, until a statue he has invited to dinner accepts and carries him off.
The Miser (1668). Harpagon loves his buried money-box above his children, and plans to marry the young woman his son loves.
The Would-Be Gentleman (1670). Monsieur Jourdain, a rich merchant, hires teachers of music, dancing, fencing and philosophy so that he can become a nobleman, and is fooled by a fake Turkish ceremony.
The Would-Be Invalid (1673). Argan is sure he is ill and wants a doctor for a son-in-law. His maid Toinette disguises herself as a doctor to cure him of doctors.

full.name: gb-moliere
full.cap: The same pattern runs through the comedies: a hero ruled by one idea, someone who sees clearly, and the people at risk.

full.html: When his money-box is stolen, Harpagon falls apart in a famous speech that ends with him suspecting everyone, even the audience:

full.text: Thieves! thieves! assassins! murder! Justice, just heavens! I am undone; I am murdered; they have cut my throat; they have stolen my money! Who can it be? What has become of him? Where is he? Where is he hiding himself? What shall I do to find him? Where shall I run? Where shall I not run? Is he not here?
full.author: Molière
full.work: The Miser, Act IV, Scene VII
full.ed: The Dramatic Works of Molière, George Bell & Sons

full.html: Earlier, the young steward Valère, who must please Harpagon to stay near the daughter he loves, praises a saying Harpagon wants carved over his fireplace:

full.text: We must eat to live, and not live to eat.
full.author: Molière
full.work: The Miser, Act III, Scene V
full.ed: The Dramatic Works of Molière, George Bell & Sons
full.note: Valère attributes it to one of the ancients

full.html: Character comedy. Molière's best plays are named after a type of person: the miser, the hypocrite, the would-be gentleman. Words like “a Tartuffe” and “a Harpagon” entered French as names for those types.
Thinking the servants are just there for jokes. Dorine, Nicole and Toinette are often the clearest-sighted people on stage, and they say what the audience is thinking.

deep.html: Tartuffe was the great battle of Molière's life. Some churchmen held that a play showing a man using religion as a mask would make audiences mock religion itself; Molière and his defenders answered that exposing false devotion protects the true kind. The king allowed public performances in 1669. Don Juan was withdrawn after a short run in 1665. Readers still debate where the line between satire of hypocrisy and satire of belief lies; the play presents the hypocrite's piety as false.

Molière, long ill, played the imaginary invalid Argan in the fourth performance of his last play in February 1673, was taken ill on stage, and died a few hours later. The French national theater, the Comédie-Française, formed from his company in 1680, is still called “the house of Molière.”

Molière's types run through later comedy in many languages, and his plays are among the most translated in the world. Compare Aristophanes' older comedy on this ladder, and the satire of Swift and Voltaire in the next era.

items: Can laughter change how people behave?
Why is it funny when someone cares too much about one thing?
Is it ever unkind to laugh at a character? Where is the line?

questions: Which of Molière's foolish heroes would be the funniest to play? Why?
Monsieur Jourdain wants to seem fancy. What do people do today to seem important?
Why do you think the servants in Molière often see the truth before their masters do?
Harpagon loves money more than his family. What do you think he should have learned?
Molière thought comedy could fix people's faults by making them laugh. Has laughing at a story ever changed what you do?
